title: Empirical Integration of a Formal Network Verifier as an Oracle inside an LLM Generate–Verify–Repair Loop: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired within‑task experiment (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1) to test whether embedding a deterministic network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded LLM Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) loop increases the proportion of unsafe or incorrect LLM‑generated network configurations that are detected/rejected and whether bounded repair recovers verifier‑accepted outputs more often than single‑shot generation. Using a synthetic intent→configuration suite (N=270 tasks), gpt-5-mini as generator (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2...), and a Dockerized Kathará/Mininet deterministic validator/emulator as ground truth, we observed no verifier rejections: baseline accepted 270/270 (100%); guarded (verify → optional bounded repair) accepted 270/270 (100%); bounded repair was not invoked. Paired difference = 0.00 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00], exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729). The run used preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false), which deterministically produced one generated candidate per paired task and is the proximate cause of the degenerate contingency. We release the full preregistration and deterministic execution bundle (preregistration SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e...a1c0; master_prompt archive provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 1872df1e...) and provide an artifact‑anchored minimal recipe to re-run the original estimand under independent sampling. All scoring JSONs, validator traces, and per‑artifact SHA‑256 hashes are archived (execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 43381c4b...).

sections.introduction: Motivation. LLM‑assisted intent→configuration pipelines promise large NetOps productivity gains but face reliability and safety challenges: stochastic generation can produce syntactically plausible yet semantically unsafe device commands. A widely proposed mitigation is a Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) architecture: (1) generate candidate configuration(s) from natural‑language intent; (2) deterministically verify candidate correctness/safety with a formal oracle; (3) if the verifier rejects, invoke a bounded repair loop that uses verifier diagnostics to guide new generation attempts. Research question. Does embedding a deterministic network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded LLM GVR loop increase detection/rejection of unsafe/incorrect generated configurations and improve bounded repair success versus single‑shot generation? Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered paired experiment with deterministic provenance (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1; preregistration SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d56671560e43f03c4a92ad5f8c9b8586ac8eb3cc3c8fa00a1c0). (2) A complete deterministic execution and scoring bundle with per‑artifact SHA‑256 hashes (example: execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 43381c4b07e1ffabb163657f56ae893fd65fc12d5307ea1ff3bb98f7cf43329a). (3) An empirical, artifact‑anchored analysis that shows how generation semantics (shared candidate vs independent sampling) control whether a verifier insertion can change measured outcomes and provides an explicit reproducible minimal change recipe to test the original estimand under independent sampling.
sections.related_work: Generate‑then‑verify architectures and GVR variants appear across domains that require constrained correctness (Cadenas, Convergent Correctness; doi:10.2139/ssrn.6754899). Formal network verification languages and decision procedures (NetKAT, weighted NetKAT family) provide deterministic oracles suitable for NetOps validators (Suárez Acevedo et al.; doi:10.1145/3808318). Recent NetOps proposals combine intent life‑cycle management, retrieval augmentation and verifier anchoring (OpenAlex records W4400072049, W4386722061, W4414359351). Prior studies mostly provide architectures, limited case studies, or single‑case evaluations; our study adds a preregistered paired design with complete deterministic logging and per‑artifact hashing to permit exact reproduction and deterministic diagnosis of why an empirical run produced its observed contingency.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen plan. The preregistration (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1) froze estimands, sampling, retry policy, and run semantics prior to execution; archived preregistration SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d56671560e43f03c4a92ad5f8c9b8586ac8eb3cc3c8fa00a1c0. Primary estimand. paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline: within‑task paired difference in proportion of verifier rejections/accepts. Design and task bank. Paired within‑task design with Npairs=270 drawn from SyntheticNetOpsIntentConfig_v1 (3 vendor syntaxes × 3 topology templates × 30 tasks). A stratified 20% validation subset (54 tasks) was reserved to compute verifier↔emulator concordance. Generator and verifier. Declared generator: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2...), provider recorded as openai_responses; deterministic verifier: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 executed against a Dockerized Kathará/Mininet emulator used as ground truth (emulator artifacts archived under execution/*). Execution contract decisive fields. The preregistration set initial_generation_calls_per_task=1 and independent_condition_generation=false (shared_initial_candidate semantics) so a single generated candidate per task was evaluated under both arms; maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1; planned_episode_count=540 (270 pairs × 2 conditions). Scoring and validator traces. Every candidate was deterministically validated and scored; scoring JSONs in execution/scoring/*.json contain validator_trace entries with normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, touched_field_count, violation codes, and final validation decisions (representative files and SHA‑256s are archived). Statistical analysis. Primary test: exact McNemar two‑sided on paired dichotomous accept/reject; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed=1729). Missingness and retries. Model call failures were handled by a preregistered deterministic retry policy (≤2 retries); all retries and any infrastructure failures were logged in execution/execution_log.jsonl. Repair policy. Guarded arm: when verifier rejected a candidate, invoke bounded repair loop using verifier diagnostics; preregistered maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1. All raw responses, repair prompts (if used), provider traces, and per‑artifact SHA‑256 manifest were archived (execution/*; full manifest referenced in execution_manifest).

Repairs invoked in guarded arm: 0 (no initial rejections; no repair calls). Verifier↔emulator concordance (validation subset): 54/54 agreement (false_accept=0, false_reject=0) as computed from the reserved validation episodes' scoring JSONs. Statistical inference. Observed paired difference = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap_resamples = 10,000; bootstrap_seed = 1729). Diagnostic interpretation. The degenerate CI and p value are arithmetic consequences of zero discordant pairs (n10=n01=0). Those inferential quantities therefore reflect the executed shared‑candidate semantics and the observed generator behavior and must not be overinterpreted as evidence that verifiers are generically useless. Each scoring JSON contains the validator_trace with parsed_command_count, normalized_configuration, and the validator decision; the example responses are stored under execution/responses/*.txt (each file hashed in the execution manifest).
sections.discussion: Why the run produced a provenance‑anchored null. Two preregistered, archived decisions produced the observed degenerate contingency: (1) the execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false) so one generated candidate per task was evaluated in both arms; and (2) with the chosen prompts and generator settings (gpt-5-mini, execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2...), the single generated candidate per task was verifier‑acceptable for every task in the supplied synthetic task bank. Both facts are archived and verifiable (execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/raw_results.jsonl). Consequence for the estimand and power. The preregistered power/MDE computation assumed independent stochastic generation per arm (independent_condition_generation=true). Because the executed run used shared candidate semantics the power/MDE assumptions do not apply; the reported p=1.0 and CI=[0.00,0.00] are therefore degenerate and should be interpreted as conditional on identical generated candidates rather than as a general null about verifier utility. Operational implications. The results identify a concrete regime: when a generation pipeline (prompt + model) produces verifier‑acceptable candidates for a task bank, inserting a deterministic verifier with a bounded repair loop will not change observed accept/reject outcomes under shared‑candidate evaluation. This is a useful boundary condition—verifiers remain necessary when generators fail or in independent‑sampling regimes, but their marginal measured effect depends on generation sampling semantics and generator failure rate. Reproducible, artifact‑anchored follow‑up recipe. To test the original preregistered estimand (marginal verifier effect under independent sampling) using the archived harness, change only the following preregistered fields and rerun the archived executor: (A) set execution_contract.independent_condition_generation = true in the preregistration/execution JSON so each arm receives an independent generation; (B) set execution_contract.maximum_model_calls or planned_model_calls ≥ 540 so model_calls_used permits one independent generation per arm per task; (C) adjust execution/model_configuration.json to introduce sampling variability (for example set temperature>0 or provide a short list of deterministic seeds in the task_manifest) so generator outputs differ across independent draws; (D) optionally set maximum_repair_calls_per_task > 1 to evaluate multi‑attempt bounded repair convergence. Exact field names and artifact paths referenced above are present in the archived execution (see execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2...). Threats to validity. Internal: shared candidate semantics removed between‑arm stochasticity; construct: synthetic tasks approximate operational patterns but do not capture full production heterogeneity; external: single generator (gpt-5-mini) and single verifier rule set limit generalizability; conclusion: zero discordant pairs prevent rejection of the preregistered null but do not imply a verifier is ineffective in other regimes.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired study integrating a deterministic network verifier into an LLM GVR pipeline and released the complete deterministic artifact bundle. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and the chosen generator/settings the single generated candidate per task was verifier‑acceptable for all N=270 tasks, so the verifier/repair path was not invoked; observed paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p=1.0). This provenance‑anchored null identifies a concrete evaluation regime in which a deterministic verifier does not change measured accept/reject outcomes. The primary methodological lesson is that generation semantics (shared candidate vs independent sampling) critically determine whether a verifier insertion is testable for the preregistered estimand. We publish the exact artifacts and provide an artifact‑grounded minimal recipe so others can deterministically explore the regime where verifier/repair utility will be observed. All raw outputs, scoring traces, and the full per‑artifact SHA‑256 manifest are released to permit deterministic reproduction (see execution/* and analysis/* in the archived bundle).

limitations: Synthetic task suite and limited operational realism: results may not generalize to complex, noisy, adversarial, or production NetOps environments; emulator behavior can differ from heterogeneous production devices.
Single‑model evaluation: only a single generator (gpt-5-mini) was used; no claim of multi‑model generality should be inferred.

Generation semantics constraint: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false) produced one generated candidate per task and thereby eliminated between‑arm stochastic sampling variance; the preregistered MDE calculations assumed independent sampling and are therefore inapplicable to the observed contingency.

Bounded repair budget: the repair loop allowed at most one repair call per rejected candidate (maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1); multi‑attempt repair strategies were not evaluated and could change outcomes.

Verifier rule‑set sensitivity: a single deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and rule set were used; different verifier conservatism or policy choices will change false‑accept/reject tradeoffs.
Emulator vs production gap: emulator‑validated safety does not guarantee identical behavior on production devices or multi‑vendor deployments.
